headline: Read the OCSP response a CMS message carries in its crls field, instead of accepting it unread.
summary: A `crls` field can carry revocation information in the `other` arm RFC 5652 sec. 10.2.1 defines, and RFC 5940 registers an OCSP response as one of its formats. This build already admitted such an entry and already required the higher SignedData version it implies, but nothing read the interior: an entry carrying arbitrary bytes parsed clean, nothing distinguished an OCSP entry from an SCVP one, and a response carried with a message could not reach revocation checking without the caller taking it apart. The entry is now read in all four content types that can carry one, its format is named, the embedded response is surfaced as a record `pki.path.ocspChecker` and `pki.path.verifyOcspResponse` take directly, and the shapes the two documents forbid are refused rather than passed along.

Added: A `crls` entry in the `other [1]` arm is read as RFC 5652 sec. 10.2.1 `OtherRevocationInfoFormat` and carries `otherRevInfoFormat` (dotted), `otherRevInfoFormatName` (or `null` for a format no registry names) and `otherRevInfoBytes`, the raw ANY TLV exactly as it arrived. A CertificateList entry is unchanged. An operator can now tell an RFC 5940 OCSP entry from an SCVP one, and either from an unregistered format, which nothing in this build could do before.

For `id-ri-ocsp-response`, the embedded OCSP response is surfaced in `ocspResponse` as a parsed record, with the byte ranges a verifier hashes left raw. `pki.path.ocspChecker`, `pki.path.verifyOcspResponse`, `pki.ocsp.verify` and `pki.lint.ocsp` all accept it as it stands: harvest the entries with `crls.map(e => e.ocspResponse).filter(Boolean)` and hand them over. The same verbs take the record and the caller re-encodes nothing; a rebuilt copy of it is refused exactly as a rebuilt parse result is.

A carried response whose `responseType` names a body this build does not decode keeps its envelope and leaves the body alone: `ocspResponse.basicResponse` is `null` and `ocspResponse.responseBytes.response` holds the bytes as they arrived. RFC 6960 sec. 4.2.1 dispatches the response body on that OID and RFC 5940 sec. 3 asks for a successful status rather than a body a reader can decode, so the message parses and a caller who only needs its signature verified is not stopped by a response type nothing in the path consults. The verbs above are handed a record with no response body and determine nothing from it, so a certificate's status stays undetermined rather than reading as good. `pki.schema.ocsp.parseResponse` still refuses the same bytes with `ocsp/unsupported-response-type`: a client that asked a responder for an answer needs to be told it cannot be read.

The same reading applies to `originatorInfo.crls`, so EnvelopedData (RFC 5652 sec. 6.1), AuthenticatedData (sec. 9.1) and AuthEnvelopedData (RFC 5083 sec. 2.1) carry it too, not SignedData alone. RFC 5940 sec. 1 names all four.
`pki.oid` resolves the two id-ri formats a reader can act on: `id-ri-ocsp-response` (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.16.2) and `id-ri-scvp` (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.16.4).

`pki.lint.cms` reports a notice when a `crls` entry carries revocation information this build does not read, naming the format, the response type where there is one, and where the entry sat. An `id-ri-ocsp-response` entry whose response was read draws nothing; one whose `responseType` named a body this build does not decode draws the notice, because the revocation information it carries went unconsulted either way.
Fixed: An `other [1]` crls entry is held to its stated shape. `OtherRevocationInfoFormat` is exactly an OBJECT IDENTIFIER and an ANY, so an empty arm, a one-element arm carrying a format and no revocation information, and an arm with a third element are each refused as `cms/bad-other-rev-info`. The one-element form is what OpenSSL both accepts and can emit, because its template marks the value optional.

An OCSP response carried in that arm must state a status. A `tryLater` or `malformed` response is a well-formed OCSPResponse that conveys no revocation information, so it is refused here as `cms/bad-ocsp-rev-info` (RFC 5940 sec. 3). `pki.schema.ocsp.parseResponse` still accepts one, because a client reading a live responder's answer needs to see it.

A BasicOCSPResponse where an OCSPResponse belongs is refused. Both are SEQUENCEs, so the confusion RFC 5126 sec. 6.3.4 invites by carrying `SEQUENCE OF BasicOCSPResponse` in a signed attribute passes any tag check and fails only on the first field, where a status is read and a ResponseData arrives.

An OCSP response placed in the CertificateList position is refused as `cms/misplaced-ocsp-response`. RFC 5940 sec. 2 states that such a response is carried in the `other` arm, and a universal SEQUENCE in `crls` was previously surfaced raw whatever it held.

A caller's decode caps reach the embedded response. The walk runs under the parse's own budget rather than starting a fresh one, so a tightened cap refuses the message with the caller's typed `cms/too-large` instead of letting the nested work run at defaults.

`pki.cms.parseCertsOnly`'s `maxCerts` bound no longer decides which messages it accepts. The bound caps the certificates and CRLs parsed and returned, but it was applied by shortening the lists before they were checked, so a cap leaving no room for the CRLs dropped a tagged entry silently: a capped reader accepted a message an uncapped reader refuses and handed back an empty CRL list where revocation information had been. The structural check now runs over every entry, and only the certificate and CRL parsing stays bounded, which is the work the bound exists for.

`pki.ocsp.verify` takes the record a `crls` entry surfaces, which it did not. Every verb that accepts a parse result re-reads it from the bytes it was parsed from, so that an edited copy cannot be verified in place of what was parsed; a record produced by walking a structure a message carries was not attributed to those bytes, so the re-reading produced an object that the next verb in the chain read as rebuilt and refused with `path/bad-input`. A record is now attributed the same way whether it was parsed from its own bytes or walked inside a message that carried it, and the refusal of a genuinely rebuilt record is unchanged.

The three readers that require a plain CertificateList still refuse a tagged entry now that a well-formed one parses: `pki.cms.parseCertsOnly` (`cms/bad-crl`), `pki.est.parseCertsOnly` (`est/bad-crl`) and a SCEP SUCCESS CertRep (`scep/bad-crl`). The SCEP refusal had no test before this change.
Changed: `pki.schema.cms.parse` reads these entries by default. An entry that was accepted unread before may now be refused if it is malformed under RFC 5652 sec. 10.2.1 or RFC 5940 sec. 3; an unrecognized format is still accepted and surfaced opaquely, because sec. 10.2.1's ANY DEFINED BY is an extension point and refusing an unknown format would refuse a future registered one. The reading is not optional, because an opt-in would leave the entry unread for every caller who does not know to ask for it.
